facts.raw_span: continuous chest pain for two hours
denied dyspnea, syncope, or prior similar episodes
no personal or family history of cardiovascular or thromboembolic disease
sinus rhythm with 2 mm of ST-segment elevation in leads V2 and V3
right ventricular dilatation and an estimated pulmonary arterial pressure of 60 mmHg
continuous chest pain for two hours
denied dyspnea, syncope, or prior similar episodes
no personal or family history of cardiovascular or thromboembolic disease
sinus rhythm with 2 mm of ST-segment elevation in leads V2 and V3
right ventricular dilatation and an estimated pulmonary arterial pressure of 60 mmHg

concepts.why: The patient presented with continuous chest pain and ST-segment elevation, which are characteristic of acute coronary syndrome.
The patient had right ventricular dilatation and an estimated pulmonary arterial pressure of 60 mmHg, indicating right ventricular dysfunction.
The patient had an estimated pulmonary arterial pressure of 60 mmHg, which is indicative of pulmonary hypertension.
The patient had ST-segment elevation and normal coronary arteries, which may indicate cardiac ischemia due to other causes.

rationales.F01: Chest pain is a common symptom of acute coronary syndrome and cardiac ischemia.
rationales.F09: ST-segment elevation is a hallmark of acute coronary syndrome and cardiac ischemia.
rationales.F10: New right bundle branch block may indicate right ventricular dysfunction.
rationales.F11: Normal coronary arteries without stenosis rule out acute coronary syndrome and cardiac ischemia.
rationales.F12: Right ventricular dilatation and elevated pulmonary arterial pressure suggest right ventricular dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension.

frontier_selector.rationale: The patient's right ventricular dilatation and estimated pulmonary arterial pressure of 60 mmHg, along with the new right bundle branch block, support Right Ventricular Dysfunction as the most fitting diagnosis.
